12	## SOC2/ISO 27001
13	### SOC 2
14	  - **Who runs it**: AICPA (American Institute of CPAs). It's a **CPA audit**, not a security cert.
15	  - **What you get**: An **attestation report** written by an auditor — not a certificate. The report is **confidential**, shared with customers under NDA.
16	  - **What it's measured against**: the **Trust Services Criteria (TSC)** — 5 categories:
17	    - **Security** (the "Common Criteria") — _mandatory, always in scope_
18	    - Availability · Processing Integrity · Confidentiality · Privacy — _optional, picked based on what you do_
19	  - **Type I vs Type II** (know this cold):
20	    - **Type I** = controls are _well-designed_ at a single **point in time**.
21	    - **Type II** = controls _operated effectively_ over a **period** (usually 3-12 months). Type II is the one that actually matters; it proves the controls work over time, not just on paper.
22	  - **Geography**: North America-centric. The default ask for US SaaS companies.
23	
24	### ISO/IEC 27001
25	 
26	  - **Who runs it**: ISO + IEC (international). Audited by an **accredited certification body**.
27	  - **What you get**: An actual **certificate**, valid **3 years** with annual surveillance audits. Publicly shareable.
28	  - **Core concept**: it's about building an **ISMS** — Information Security Management System. The standard cares less about a fixed checklist and more about whether you have a _living, risk-based management_ _process_ (Plan-Do-Check-Act continual improvement).
29	  - **Controls**: **Annex A**. The current **2022** version has **93 controls in 4 themes** (Organizational, People, Physical, Technological). _(The older 2013 version had 114 controls across 14 domains — mention "2022"_ _so you sound current.)_
30	  - **Geography**: the **international** standard. What European/global customers expect.
31	### How to sound fluent
32	
33	  - "They overlap heavily — roughly 80% of the controls map to each other — which is why mature orgs like TRM hold **both**: SOC 2 Type II for US customers, ISO 27001 for international, plus FedRAMP High for federal."
34	  - "The mental model I use: **SOC 2 proves your controls work; ISO 27001 proves you have a system for managing security as an ongoing process.**"
35	  - The honest-gap line for TRM: _"I haven't owned a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 audit cycle myself — my exposure is conceptual through Sec+ and the framework structure. That's the connection that lands.

39	### **NIST CSF 2.0 (Cybersecurity Framework)**
40	
41	Released **Feb 2024**. Big v2.0 change: added **Govern** as a 6th function and expanded scope beyond critical infrastructure to _all_ orgs.
42	
43	**Six Functions** (mnemonic order — Govern wraps the other five):
44	
45	  - **GOVERN** _(new)_ — risk strategy, roles/responsibilities, policy, oversight, **supply-chain risk (C-SCRM)**. The "set the strategy and hold people accountable" function.
46	  - **IDENTIFY** — know your assets, risks, environment. Can't protect what you can't see.
47	  - **PROTECT** — safeguards: **IAM/access control**, training, data security, platform security. _(This is your wheelhouse — identity lives here.)_
48	  - **DETECT** — continuous monitoring, find anomalies/events.
49	  - **RESPOND** — incident management, analysis, mitigation, comms.
50	  - **RECOVER** — restore operations, recovery comms.
51	
52	**Three components beyond the Core:**
53	
54	  - **Implementation Tiers (1-4)**: Partial → Risk-Informed → Repeatable → Adaptive. How mature/rigorous your risk practices are.
55	  - **Profiles**: Current ("where we are") vs Target ("where we want to be") — the gap between them = your roadmap.
56	  - It's **voluntary and outcome-based** — it tells you _what_ to achieve, not _how_. That flexibility is the whole point.
57	### **NIST AI RMF 1.0 (AI Risk Management Framework)**
58	
59	Released **Jan 2023**; **Generative AI Profile** added **July 2024**. Voluntary, like CSF.
60	
61	**Four Core Functions** (Govern is again the cross-cutting one):
62	  - **GOVERN** — culture, policies, accountability structures. Informs all the others.
63	  - **MAP** — establish context, frame and categorize the AI system's risks.
64	  - **MEASURE** — assess/analyze/track risks with metrics, testing, evaluation.
65	  - **MANAGE** — prioritize, allocate resources, respond, recover.
66	
67	**7 characteristics of "trustworthy AI"** (the goal the framework drives toward):
68	Valid & reliable (foundational) · Safe · Secure & resilient · Accountable & transparent · Explainable & interpretable · Privacy-enhanced · Fair with harmful bias managed.
69

This is where you mine him for *exactly how to win the final round* and quietly manage the offer mechanics. Recruiters are on your side at this stage — Josh advancing you makes him look good, so he'll usually tell you how to succeed if you ask the right way.

Here's what I'd walk in with, grouped by what you're actually trying to get out of him:

**1. De-risk the final round (your highest-value questions)**
- "What does the final round look like — format, how long, and who will I be meeting with?" (Get **names and roles** so I can build you a quick dossier on each.)
- "What are they primarily evaluating in this last round? Is it more technical depth, team fit, or something else?"
- "Is there anything from my earlier conversations with you and Dustin you'd suggest I lean into or expand on?" — this is the killer. It surfaces any soft reservations *before* the final, while you can still fix them. Earlier notes flagged you undersold Azure/Entra depth with Josh and never nailed down the CST→EST commitment — this is your chance to hear if either is lingering.

**2. The money clock (don't skip this)**
Your screen notes say the **performance bonus requires a start date before June 30** (payout in January). It's June 3 and the final isn't even scheduled yet — final → offer → accept → onboard in under 4 weeks is tight. Worth asking plainly:
- "When we talked, there was a performance bonus tied to starting before June 30 — given where we are in the process, is that window still realistic, or has it shifted?"

That's real money *and* it gives you a legitimate, non-pushy reason to ask him to keep the process moving fast.

**3. Comp (gentle setup, not a hard negotiation)**
Your notes flag that you said the $105–115K range was "acceptable" but **never anchored at the top**. You don't negotiate with the recruiter on a Q&A call, but you can plant the flag:
- "Is the comp band location-adjusted or flat across the US?" (You're CST — worth knowing.)
- And if comp comes up naturally: signal IC3 / senior-IC framing so $115K reads as the obvious landing spot, not the ceiling you're grateful to reach.

**4. Two human/culture questions to close warm**
- "What's the team's working rhythm actually like day to day? The 'high-velocity, high-ownership' language comes up a lot — I want to make sure I'm picturing it accurately." (Pressure-tests the startup-intensity flag in your notes without sounding scared of it.)
- "What's something about working at TRM that surprised you?"

text: How is this for the personal interests answer: I organize the local Kansas City Effective Altruism community; we host book clubs, workshops, educational talks, and discussion groups on philosophy, ethics, philanthropy, and critical thinking. I also am a huge AI enthusiast and am almost always building something with Claude to improve my life, whether it's integrating more systems together, or creating an app to make Dungeons and Dragons easier to play. I'm also high energy and very social; I thrive when I'm working with people or spending time with friends, so I can often be found at coffee shops coworking with groups of 3-5 other people.

blocks.text:
Honestly? It's a strong answer. It does three things your form needs: it shows **leadership** (organizing a community backs up your #2 motivator), it shows **social/collaborative energy** (great signal for their fast, high-ownership culture), and the AI/D&D detail is authentically *you* and ties straight to TRM using Claude. The "coworking at coffee shops with 3-5 people" is a great specific, human touch. Keep that.

One thing I want to flag — not to talk you out of it, just so you walk in aware and it's a deliberate choice:

**TRM is a crypto-crime-tracing company, and EA has an FTX-shaped shadow in exactly that world.** Sam Bankman-Fried was EA's most public figure, FTX was crypto fraud, and tracing that kind of fraud is literally TRM's business. To a TRM interviewer, "I organize the EA community… philanthropy" *could* pattern-match to SBF before it matches to "thoughtful, mission-driven person." It probably won't — these are sophisticated people who know EA isn't FTX — but it's the one place in your answer where the reader's brain might go somewhere you didn't intend.

You've got three ways to play it, all fine:

1. **Keep it exactly as is.** It's true, it's a real leadership credential, and being openly EA at a mission-driven firm is arguably a *plus*. Just be ready to talk about it warmly if it comes up.
2. **Keep EA, drop "philanthropy."** That one word is what most directly trips the FTX wire. "Philosophy, ethics, and critical thinking" carries the same meaning without the crypto-charity echo.
3. **Lead with the leadership, soften the label.** e.g. *"I organize a local Kansas City discussion community built around philosophy, ethics, and critical thinking — book clubs, workshops, talks."* Same substance, less brand baggage.

My pick would be **#2** — you keep your identity and your leadership story intact, you just remove the one word most likely to misfire in this specific room. Lightly tightened:

> I organize the Kansas City Effective Altruism community, hosting book clubs, workshops, talks, and discussion groups on philosophy, ethics, and critical thinking. I'm also a huge AI enthusiast and am almost always building something with Claude to improve my life, whether that's tying more of my systems together or making an app to make Dungeons & Dragons easier to run. And I'm high-energy and social: I do my best work around people, so you'll often find me coworking with a group of 3-5 at a coffee shop.

Your call entirely though — if being upfront about EA feels right to you (and there's a real case that it does at a mission company), keep #1 and own it.

**Grammar fix:** "as well Nerdio" → "as well **as** Nerdio." And I'd add one strategic closer. Polished:

> I'm also interviewing with Coefficient Giving for their IT Associate role, and with Nerdio for their Support Solutions Engineer role. I'm being selective rather than applying broadly, and TRM is the opportunity I'm most excited about.

That last clause isn't fluff — it's true (mission is your #1 motivator) and it tells Josh you're a real flight risk to *other* offers while signaling TRM is your top choice. That's exactly the message that makes a recruiter push to keep things moving (and protect your June-30 bonus window).

**Optional — add stage for urgency.** If you want to crank the "move quickly" signal, you can note where each stands, e.g. *"Nerdio I just completed a first interview; Coefficient is at the work-test stage."* It shows momentum. Downside: it also reveals you don't have an offer in hand yet. For a pre-final form I'd lean toward keeping it simple as above and letting "I'm most excited about TRM" do the work — but it's your call if you want more pressure on the timeline.

**One heads-up, tying back to the EA conversation:** *Coefficient Giving is the rebranded Open Philanthropy* — i.e., it's an EA grantmaking org. So naming it here quietly reinforces the EA association we just talked about softening in your interests answer. That's not a reason to hide it (it's the honest truth and a totally normal place to be interviewing), just something to be aware of: if you're consciously down-playing the EA brand in one answer, you're re-introducing it in another. Whoever reads the full form sees both. Personally I think it's fine — it's a real role and a fair answer — but you wanted me being the one watching the whole board, so there it is.

text: What about this answer to the 2nd interview process question: Yes, I expect to at least receive an offer from Coefficient Giving by mid/late July, although I'm going to ask them to expedite that.

blocks.text:
This one I'd actually pump the brakes on, for two reasons — one honesty, one strategy.

**1. "I expect to at least receive an offer" overstates where you are.** Coefficient is at the *work-test* stage. That's genuinely advanced, but it's not "offer incoming" — you still have to clear the work test and whatever follows. Stating you *expect* an offer is a confidence claim you can't fully back, and if you're the kind of person who just flagged the AI-tool honesty thing, this is the same muscle. Recruiters also have a good nose for inflated competing-offers. Calibrate it to what's true and it's actually *more* credible, not less.

**2. The July timeline quietly works against your June 30 bonus.** Think about what Josh does with "offer expected mid/late July": he concludes *TRM has until July to get you an offer out.* That's the opposite of the pressure you want — your bonus needs you **started before June 30**, which means offer + accept weeks earlier than that. Citing a July competing offer hands TRM permission to slow-walk right past your bonus window. The lever for June 30 isn't a competing offer; it's asking Josh directly to keep the process moving because of the bonus. Don't let this answer undercut that.

**3. Drop "I'm going to ask them to expedite."** It's too much inside-baseball, it reads slightly as gaming the timeline, and it undercuts your own stated date (if you're expediting, "mid/late July" isn't real). Keep your machinery out of view.

Calibrated rewrite:

> I don't have a signed offer in hand yet. My process with Coefficient Giving is at an advanced stage and could produce an offer in the coming weeks. I'll flag any firm offer or deadline to you the moment it appears. For my part, I'm ready to move quickly and TRM is my top choice.
